4 · The same news, framed four ways.

I’ve tried three times.  →  the count, finished.

1 · Read the explanation.
Why the phone runs on the present perfect

A telephone call is a period of time that is still open while you are in it. That is why so much phone language uses the present perfect: It’s been great talking to you, you’ve caught me at a bad time, I’ve been trying to reach you. Each one connects something that started earlier to the moment you are speaking.

The moment the call ends, the frame changes. In the follow-up email you write It was good to speak to you, because the call is now a finished event in the past.

Three choices you have to make
  • Simple or continuous? I’ve tried three times (a count, finished) against I’ve been trying all morning (the effort, still running).
  • Present perfect or past simple? A finished time expression forces the past simple: I called you at nine, never I’ve called you at nine.
  • Reason before action. Across all four recorded calls, whoever refuses, delays or ends a call gives a reason first: I’m still at the office and I’ve got a ton of work to do — I’d better get off the phone. The grammar is only half of it; the order is the other half.

Two things to watch

1 — Have got is a present, not a perfect. I’ve got a ton of work describes now, not the past. It cannot become I’ve been getting a ton of work without changing the meaning entirely.

2 — The tense follows the moment of speaking. The same call is it’s been great while you are on it and it was great five minutes later. Neither is more polite; they belong to different moments.

10 · Read this before the extra practice.
Why a phone call is full of present perfect

A call is a period that is still open while you are in it, so the tense that joins past to present does the functional work. I’ve been trying to reach you all morning gives a reason by pointing at the activity that filled the period. You’ve caught me at a bad time reports a single recent action whose result is now. It’s been great talking to you closes the call by treating it as a period that is just ending — which is why it is not It was great until after you hang up.

Once the call is over it becomes a closed event and the past simple takes over: I spoke to her yesterday, She rang twice while you were out. Mixing the two is the commonest error on this lesson: I have spoken to her yesterday.

Doing things with the tense

Giving a reason to end: I’ve got a lot on · I’ve been meaning to catch up with the report all day. Softening the exit: I won’t keep you · I’ll let you get on · I won’t take up any more of your time. Apologising for a delay: Sorry, I’ve only just seen your message. Leaving a message: I’ve tried your mobile twice — could you call me back?

Register matters as much as form. Contractions (I’ve, it’s) are normal on almost every call; the full forms sound cold except in a formal complaint. And note that just, already and yet travel with the simple form: I’ve just got out of a meeting, Have they replied yet?

Errors to watch: I am trying to reach you since this morning → I’ve been trying since this morning · It has been great to talk to you yesterday → It was great… · I have called you two hours ago → I called you two hours ago.

Hi Sam,

I’ve been meaning to write for ages and then leaving it, which is exactly what I always do. Anyway, two things.

First, the job: I got it. I’m over the moon, and also quietly terrified, because I start in three weeks and I’ve done nothing about finding somewhere to live. If you know anybody in Cardiff, do copy me in on the conversation.

Second, and this is the reason I finally sat down to write: I watched a documentary about the other languages of Britain last night and I have not stopped thinking about it. Around 560,000 people speak Welsh — about a fifth of Wales — and roughly 40 per cent of children there have some. Cornish is the strange one. The last native speaker died more than two centuries ago and the language survived only in the names of hills and coves, and now three to five hundred people speak it fluently again.

How is the new place? Ring me when you have a free evening — the coverage at my flat is dreadful, so try the landline.
